content: 1. In 1979, a study in Thailand compared three different strategies for nutritional rehabilitation in managing moderate acute malnutrition among children aged 6 to 24 months. This was a multicenter, randomized controlled trial conducted as part of the MALINEA project. 2. A 2018 study by Vray M, Hedible BG, Adam P, and colleagues demonstrated that plasma beta-carotene and retinol concentrations in children increased after a 30-day supplementation with the fruit Momordica cochinchinensis (commonly known as gac). 3. Research conducted in 1996 by Walker SP, Grantham-McGregor SM, Himes JH, and others found that early childhood supplementation did not provide long-term growth benefits for stunted children in Jamaica. 4. A 2013 investigation by Wang RJ, Trehan I, LaGrone LN, and colleagues explored the acceptability of food and feeding practices for lipid-based nutrient supplements and blended flours used to treat moderate malnutrition. 5. In 1993, Walter TD, Bartholmey S, and Arredondo M evaluated the effectiveness of iron-fortified infant cereal in preventing iron deficiency anemia in infants. 6. A 2016 study by Whitfield KC, Karakochuk CD, and colleagues showed that consuming thiamin-fortified fish sauce improved thiamin status in rural Cambodian women of childbearing age and their children under 5 years old. 7. Another study by Whitfield KC and colleagues in 2016 demonstrated that household consumption of thiamin-fortified fish sauce increased erythrocyte thiamin concentrations among rural Cambodian women and their children under 5 years old in a randomized controlled trial. 8. Research by Westcott JE, Culbertson D, Lei S, and others in 2011 emphasized the critical role of complementary food choices in meeting physiological zinc requirements. 9. A global network cluster randomized controlled trial in 2010, involving institutions like the Kinshasa School of Public Health and Aga Khan University, examined complementary feeding practices under the First Bites initiative. 10. A 2000 study by Yeung GS and Zlotkin SH assessed the efficacy of meat and iron-fortified commercial cereal in preventing iron depletion in cow milk-fed infants aged 6 to 12 months. 11. Ying C and colleagues in 1956 investigated the relationship between diet and infant growth during the weaning period (6–18 months). 12. A 2013 study by Yu D, Ma G, and others evaluated the effects of three nutrition interventions on children's growth, hemoglobin concentration, and anemia in poor rural areas of China. 13. Yuliarti K, Honoris E, and Sjarif D in 2017 compared chicken liver to fortified rice cereal as a first complementary food for breastfed infants, focusing on zinc intake and status. 14. Zakaria, Rauf S, and Salim A in 2019 developed an instant powder formula with added Moringa oleifera as a complementary food for infants aged 6–12 months. 15. In 2020, Zakaria, Rauf S, Salim A, and Rahman N created an instant powder with Moringa oleifera leaf powder as a complementary food for infants aged 6–12 months. 16. Zavaleta N, Kvistgaard AS, and colleagues in 2011 evaluated the efficacy of a milk fat globule membrane (MFGM)-enriched complementary food in reducing diarrhea, anemia, and improving micronutrient status in infants. 17. Zhang Y, Wu Q, and others in 2016 studied the effectiveness of complementary food supplements and dietary counseling on anemia and stunting in children aged 6–23 months in poor areas of Qinghai Province, China. 18. Zhichien HE in 1956 examined the influence of weaning food on the growth of breastfed infants. 19. Ziegler EE, Nelson SE, and Jeter JM in 2009 found that the iron status of breastfed infants improved equally with medicinal iron and iron-fortified cereal. 20. In 2011, Ziegler EE, Nelson SE, and Jeter JM reviewed the benefits of iron supplementation for breastfed infants. 21. Zyba SJ, Wegmuller R, and colleagues in 2019 investigated the effect of exogenous phytase added to small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) on zinc absorption from millet-based porridge consumed with SQ-LNS in young Gambian children.
